AWARD 1.

The present Detailed Accident Report (hereinafter "DAR") was filed by the investigating officer,
PSI Rakesh Kumar, in FIR number 253 dated 18.04.2019, lodged at Police Station Uttam Nagar under Sections 279/337 of the IPC regarding the injuries suffered by the petitioner, Sh. Kishan Gupta, in a road accident involving a motorcycle bearing registration number DL 4SAZ 3502.
The DAR was treated as a claim petition under Section 166(4) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (hereinafter "MV Act").

1.1 The respondent no. 1, Sh. Pankaj Kaushik, is the driver and the respondent no. 2, Sh. B.R.
Kaushik, is the owner of the said motorcycle.

The respondent no. 1 is also the son of respondent no.
2.
DAR 2.

As per the DAR, on 16.04.2019 at about 12:30 a.m., the petitioner, along with his friend Sh.
Chandan, was returning on a bicycle after attending a function on Shani Bazar Road, Uttam Nagar.

The petitioner was riding the bicycle, while Sh. Chandan was seated on it.

At that time, a motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502, being driven by respondent no. 1 at high speed, in a rash,
negligent and zig-zag manner, hit their bicycle.
As a consequence, the petitioner, Sh. Chandan, and respondent no. 1 sustained injuries.

All three were taken to Deen Dayal Upadhyay (DDU) Hospital,
Delhi, for their medical treatment.

Subsequently, the petitioner was taken to Safdarjung Hospital,
Delhi where he received treatment.
Defence of the Respondents 3.
Notice of the DAR was served on the respondents.
3.1 Respondent nos. 1 and 2 filed a common reply wherein they, inter alia, denied the occurrence of the accident with the alleged offending motorcycle.
They further contended that the police has filed a false and frivolous case against them and that there is no truth in the DAR.
They further claimed that the offending motorcycle was duly insured and that respondent no. 1 was holding a valid driving licence at the relevant time.
Inquiry 4. After completion of the pleadings, following issues were framed on 18.10.2022 by my learned predecessor:

(1) Whether petitioner sustained injuries in a motor vehicle accident dated 16.04.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of a vehicle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502 being driven by Sh. Pankaj Kaushik respondent no. 1 and owned by Sh.
B.R. Kaushik respondent no. 2?

OPP.

5.
In order to prove his claim, the petitioner examined himself as PW1 and tendered his evidence by way of affidavit and the same is exhibited as Ex. PW1/A. 5.1
In his evidence by way of affidavit, the petitioner deposed regarding the manner of the accident in line with the contents of the DAR.
Petitioner deposed that on 16.04.2019 at about 12:30 am, he, along with his friend Sh. Chandan, was returning on a bicycle after attending a function.

When they reached near Toni Cycle Store at Shani Bazar Road, a motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502, being driven at high speed, in a rash, negligent and zig-zag manner, hit their bicycle.
Resultantly, they fell down and he received multiple injuries.
He further deposed that he was a student at the time of the accident and that his studies were adversely affected due to the injuries suffered.
He deposed regarding the expenses incurred on his treatment.
5.2 Petitioner has relied on the following documents in support of his testimony:
Ex. PW1/1 is the set of his treatment record and medical bills.
Ex. PW1/2 is the DAR.

5.3 In his cross examination, he deposed that the accident took place as he was taking left turn towards Shani Bazar Road.
The respondent no. 1 had hit the bicycle from the front side.
He further deposed that respondent no. 1 was driving his motorcycle at high speed and coming from wrong side.
He deposed that the public had made the call to the police.
He denied the suggestions that he and Sh. Chandan had consumed alcohol at the party or that the accident was caused due to any negligence on his part.
6. After completion of petitioner's evidence, the matter was fixed for respondents' evidence.
7. The respondents did not examine any witness.

8. I have heard learned counsels Sh. R.K. Singh for the petitioner and Sh.
Pravesh Sharma for the respondent nos. 1 & 2.
I have perused the record.

My issue-wise findings are as under:
Issue No. 1:
Whether petitioner sustained injuries in a motor vehicle accident dated 16.04.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of a vehicle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502 being driven by Sh. Pankaj Kaushik respondent no. 1 and owned by Sh. B.R. Kaushik respondent no. 2?

OPP. 
9. Onus to prove this issue was on the petitioner.
The petitioner has relied on his testimony as well as the DAR.

10. Learned counsel for the respondents opposed the claim, contending that no accident took place with the alleged offending motorcycle and that the police has falsely implicated the respondents by filing a false and frivolous case.
He further contended that petitioner and his friend Sh. Chandan were under the influence of alcohol.

11. Before dealing with the contentions of the learned counsel for respondents, it will be worth to take a brief look at the legal position regarding the standard of proof required to be met by the petitioner, in an accident case, before a claims tribunal.

12. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bimla Devi and Others vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and Others (2009) 13 SCC 530 has held:
"15.In a situation of this nature, the Tribunal has rightly taken a holistic view of the matter.

entities.text: Bimla Devi and Others vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and Others (2009) 13 SCC 530
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was necessary to be borne in mind that strict proof of an accident caused by Kishan Gupta vs Pankaj Kaushik on 23 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36241194/
3
a particular bus in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the claimants.
The claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability.
The standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt could not have been applied.
For the said purpose, the High Court should have taken into consideration the respective stories set forth by both the parties."

13. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mangla Ram vs. Oriental Insurance Company Limited and Others (2018) 5 Supreme Court Cases 656 has laid down in paragraphs 27 & 28:
"27.

entities.text: Mangla Ram vs. Oriental Insurance Company Limited and Others (2018) 5 Supreme Court Cases 656
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: ...This Court in a recent decision in Dulcina Fernandes, noted that the key of negligence on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle as set up by the claimants was required to be decided by the Tribunal on the touchstone of preponderance of probability and certainly not by standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Suffice it to observe that the exposition in the judgments already adverted to by us, filing of charge-sheet against Respondent 2 prima facie points towards his complicity in driving the vehicle negligently and rashly.

Further, even when the accused were to be acquitted in the criminal case, this Court opined that the same may be of no effect on the assessment of the liability required in respect of motor accident cases by the Tribunal.
28. Reliance placed upon the decisions in Minu B. Mehta and Meena Variyal, by the respondents, in our opinion, is of no avail.
The dictum in these cases is on the matter in issue in the case concerned.
Similarly, even the dictum in Surender Kumar Arora will be of no avail.

In the present case, considering the entirety of the pleadings,
evidence and circumstances on record and in particular the finding recorded by the Tribunal on the factum of negligence of Respondent 2, the driver of the offending jeep, the High Court committed manifest error in taking a contrary view which, in our opinion, is an error apparent on the face of record and manifestly wrong."

14. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Smt. Pushpa Rana &
Others 2008 (101) DRJ 645

Others 2008 (101) DRJ 645

has held:
"12.

The last contention of the appellant insurance company is that the respondents claimants should have proved negligence on the part of the driver and in this regard the counsel has placed reliance on the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal; 2007 (5) SCALE 269.

entities.text: Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal; 2007 (5) SCALE 269
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: These documents are sufficient proofs to reach the conclusion that the driver was negligent.
Proceedings under Motor Vehicles Act are not akin to proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not required to be followed in this regard.
Hence, this contention of the counsel for the appellant also falls face down.
There is ample evidence on record to prove negligence on the part of the driver."

15. It is clear from the above discussed authoritative pronouncements that in a claim petition under MV Act, strict proof of an accident caused by particular vehicle in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the petitioner.
The petitioner is merely to establish his case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability.
Filing of charge-sheet against the driver prima facie points towards his complicity in driving the vehicle negligently and rashly.
Further, even if the driver were to be acquitted in the criminal case, the same may be of no effect on the assessment of the liability required in respect of motor accident cases by the Tribunal.
The Tribunal must take a holistic view of the matter.
16. The issue of negligence on the part of respondent no. 1 is to be examined in the light of the evidence brought on record.

16.1 In the present case, the accident took place on 16.04.2019 and the FIR no.
253 of 2019 was lodged by Sh. Chandan on 18.04.2019 at Police Station Uttam Nagar.

16.2 On completion of investigation, the police filed the charge-sheet against the respondent no. 1 under Sections 279/337/338 of the IPC showing the involvement of offending motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502.
16.3

In the criminal case arising out of the accident, the learned MM-08, South- West Dwarka, New Delhi, vide order dated 09.06.2022 passed in Cr. Case no. 57616/2021 titled as State vs. Pankaj Kaushik, has framed charges against the respondent no. 1 for the offences punishable under Sections 279/337/338 of the IPC and 146/196 MV Act.
16.4 The arrest memo dated 20.04.2019 shows that the respondent no. 1 was arrested in the criminal case related to the accident.

16.5 The respondent no. 2, in his reply to the notice dated 19.04.2019 under Section 133, MV Act issued to him, admitted that the offending motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502 was being driven by respondent no. 1 on the day of accident.
In his reply, he further admitted that the offending motorcycle was uninsured.
16.6 The Mechanical Inspection Report dated 22.04.2019 of the offending motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502 clearly show that the motorcycle suffered fresh damage.

5 16.7
As per the charge-sheet and the seizure memo dated 16.04.2019, the said offending motorcycle was seized by SI Kulbir from the spot of accident.
16.8 The deposition of the petitioner regarding the accident and negligence of the respondent no. 1 is largely consistent.
16.9 The medical documents produced by the petitioner further lend credence to the DAR.
The Registration Card dated 16.04.2019 of DDU Hospital, pertaining to the petitioner, shows that he was brought with history of road accident and his MLC no. 2985 was prepared.
Thereafter, he was referred to Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi for further treatment including NCCT head.

As per the Report dated 16.04.2019 of the X-ray department and CT/MR Scan Report of Safdarjung Hospital, the petitioner was diagnosed with comminuted fracture of bilateral nasal bones, comminuted fracture of bony walls of left nasolacrimal duct and bilateral cribriform plate, and fracture of medial wall of left maxillary sinus with left maxillary hemosinus.
16.10As per MLC no. 3205 dated 16.04.2019 of DDU Hospital, Delhi, pertaining to Sh. Chandan, he sustained grievous injuries in a road accident.
The MLC no. 2986 dated 16.04.2019 of DDU Hospital, Delhi, pertaining to respondent no.1, records that he too received grievous injury in a road accident.
16.11 The respondents have not led any evidence in support of the contentions raised by them in their reply.

16.12 In view of the aforesaid unimpeached documentary and oral evidence on record, plea of the learned counsel for the respondents that no accident took place with the alleged offending motorcycle is hollow and liable to be rejected outrightly.

16.13 As regards the contention of the learned counsel for the respondents that the police has falsely implicated the respondents, no complaint whatsoever has been lodged by the respondents at any stage before any senior police authority or court alleging false implication or fabrication of the case by the police.

16.14 As regards the contention of the learned counsel for the respondents that the petitioner and Sh. Chandan were under the influence of alcohol, there is nothing in the MLC of the petitioner, nor is there any other material on record, to indicate that either the petitioner or Sh. Chandan were under the influence of alcohol.

17. Taking a holistic view, it stands proved, on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities, that the accident in question was caused due to rash and negligent driving of motorcycle bearing registration no. DL 4SAZ 3502, being driven by respondent no. 1, Sh. Pankaj Kaushik, and owned by respondent no. 2, Sh. B.R. Kaushik, thereby causing grievous injuries to the petitioner.
Issue no. 1 is therefore decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

19. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC 343 has laid down the general principles relating to compensation in injury cases and held:
"6.

entities.text: Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life."

The petitioner, in his evidence by way of affidavit, has claimed that he spent 1,00,000/- on medicines and treatment and 60,000/- on physiotherapy.
The treatment record and medical bills of the petitioner (Ex. PW1/1) shows that he received most of his treatment at Safdarjung Hospital, which is a government hospital.
He has not produced any physiotherapy bill.
The original medical bills placed on record by the petitioner amount to 2000/-.
In view of this Tribunal, the petitioner is entitled only to payment towards original medical bills produced by him.

Therefore, the petitioner is entitled to 2000/- under the head medicines and treatment.
21.

The petitioner, in his evidence by way of affidavit, has further claimed that he spent 60,000/-
on conveyance and 60,000/- on special diet.
However, no documentary proof has been placed on record in support of the said claims.
Nonetheless, having regard to the fact that the petitioner suffered fracture of nasal bones, it can reasonably be inferred that he must have incurred expenses on special diet.
Since the petitioner has suffered grievous injuries, therefore, he would have incurred expenses on conveyance.
Accordingly, a sum of 15,000/- is awarded towards special diet and 10,000/- towards conveyance.
22. The petitioner, in his evidence by way of affidavit, has claimed a sum of 60,000/- towards attendant.
However, no documentary proof has been produced to establish that any attendant was hired.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
The last contention of the appellant insurance company is that the respondents claimants should have proved negligence on the part of the driver and in this regard the counsel has placed reliance on the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal; 2007 (5) SCALE 269.
On perusal of the award of the Tribunal, it becomes clear that the wife of the deceased had produced (i) certified copy of the criminal record of criminal case in FIR No. 955/2004, pertaining to involvement of the offending vehicle, (ii) criminal record showing completion of investigation of police and issue of charge sheet under Section 279/304-A,IPC against the driver;

4 (iii) certified copy of FIR, wherein criminal case against the driver was lodged; and (iv) recovery memo and mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle and vehicle of the deceased.
The petitioner was a minor at the time of accident and had suffered grievous injuries.
It is reasonable to infer that some family member would have attended to him.
Loss of schooling/studies (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured 23.
The petitioner, in his evidence by way of affidavit, has claimed that he was a student at the time of the accident.
However, he has neither produced the attendance register nor examined any witness from his school to establish that he had missed classes on account of the injury.
24. Considering that the petitioner sustained grievous injuries, it is reasonable to infer that he would have missed school and thereby suffered loss of studies.
Accordingly, the petitioner is awarded a lumpsum amount of  30,000/- under the head loss of schooling/studies.
